summary:
Lunaris is an interactive lunar south-pole mission planning and site-comparison tool designed to make landing-site information easier to understand. Missions near the Moon’s south pole face challenges: sunlight can be limited by rugged terrain, while the lunar surface can block direct communication with Earth. These conditions affect power planning, mission operations, and the selection of suitable landing regions.

Lunaris brings key information together in one interface. Its interactive 3D Moon allows users to explore candidate regions, select locations, and examine the positions of the Sun and Earth for a chosen date and time. Users can compare sites, review sunlight and Earth visibility, explore modeled communication opportunities, estimate solar-power potential and periods of darkness, and view site-by-date visibility windows. A recommendation system provides a preliminary score based on solar access, Earth visibility, and terrain indicators. The platform also includes educational resources and an exportable mission-screening report.

The project uses NASA lunar imagery and topographic data, including Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter and LOLA products, alongside astronomical calculations. Lunaris is a decision-support prototype, not a certified navigation system or live telemetry service. By presenting trade-offs clearly, it aims to help planners, students, and the public explore lunar landing challenges and make informed early-stage comparisons.
details:
Project Details – Lunaris

We created Lunaris because we wanted to make exploring the Moon's south pole easier to understand and more interesting. One of the biggest challenges of planning lunar missions is finding a suitable landing location. Some areas receive very little sunlight, while others may not have a clear view of Earth, making communication difficult. These are important factors that need to be considered before a mission can take place.

Lunaris brings these factors together in one interactive platform. Users can explore a 3D model of the Moon, choose different landing locations, and see how the positions of the Sun and Earth change over time. They can also simulate a 60-day period, check sunlight availability, examine communication opportunities, estimate solar-power potential, and compare different landing sites. We also developed a recommendation system that helps users evaluate locations based on several factors. To make the results easier to use, the platform allows users to export reports and share their selected scenarios.

We built the project using React, JavaScript, Three.js, and Vite. For astronomical calculations, we used Astronomy Engine, while NASA's lunar imagery and LOLA topographic data help us represent the Moon and its terrain.

What makes Lunaris different is that it combines several useful features in one place instead of making users switch between different tools. We wanted to create something that is not only useful for early mission research but also simple enough for students and anyone interested in space exploration to use.

Although Lunaris is still a prototype and not a certified navigation system, we hope it can help people better understand the challenges of future lunar missions.
dataRefs: Uses a locally bundled NASA LRO color map, NASA SDO/HMI Sun observation, and local Earth day, night, cloud, and relief maps. The detailed NASA topography model is larger and remains optional; the textured sphere stays available if it cannot load.
The explorer uses a bundled NASA SDO/HMI continuum image snapshot for the Sun texture. It is an observation, not a live feed. The Sun’s position in the 3D scene is computed from the selected time.
The explorer compares mean diameters from NASA planetary fact sheets: Moon 3,474.8 km, Earth 12,742 km, and Sun 1,391,400 km. The interactive scene itself is not drawn to orbital scale.
Chandrayaan‑3 and IM‑2 history links are sourced from ISRO and NASA. Blue Ghost 1 is shown as context, not as a south-pole landing.
Computed with astronomy-engine (IAU lunar rotation model), checked against lunar libration. Without terrain, yearly sunlight is close to 50% at every polar site; terrain is what separates them.

Implemented for the catalog sites inside 80°S: a 360° horizon mask ray-marched 150 km over the LRO LOLA polar DEM LDEM_80S_80M (80 m/px, PDS Geosciences Node), seen from a 2 m mast. Sun and Earth count as up when their centre clears that horizon. Chandrayaan-3 and free-clicked points keep the smooth horizon, and features smaller than 80 m are not resolved.
